East Sussex is a county in South East England. It is bordered by the counties of Kent to the north and east, Surrey to the north west and West Sussex to the west, and to the south by the English Channel.
East Sussex is part of the ancient kingdom of the South Saxons, who established themselves there in the fifth century AD, after the departure of the Romans, and absorbed the remaining British population. Archaeological remains are plentiful, especially in the upland areas. The area's position on the coast has also meant that there were many invaders, including the Romans and later the Normans. Earlier industries have included fishing, iron-making, and the wool trade, all of which have declined, or disappeared. Sussex is traditionally sub-divided into six rapes. From the 12th century the three eastern rapes together formed the county of Sussex and became a single administrative area under an elected county council in 1889. Until 1974, the county was divided into the administrative counties of East Sussex and West Sussex.
East Sussex has a greater proportion of land on the South Downs than any other county in the UK. The highest point in the South Downs and the county is Ditchling Beacon, at 248 metres (814 ft). About 20% of the county is within the South Downs National Park. The Weald occupies the northern borderlands of the county – between the Downs and the county of Kent, and the Low Weald stretches across the centre of the county. Rivers in the county include the River Ouse, River Adur, River Cuckmere, River Uck, and various smaller tributaries. A large part of the population lives in the coastal strip to the south; the largest town in the county is the seaside resort of Brighton and Hove.

The Teatro Real in Madrid has just announced its 2015-16 season, and it includes a new production of Vicente Martín y Soler's Una cosa rara, directed by Emilio Sagi and conducted by Jesús López Cobos.
The opera was first performed in 1786 at the Burgtheater in Vienna, and was a great success. It was the first of three collaborations between Martín y Soler and Lorenzo da Ponte, who also wrote the librettos for Mozart's Don Giovanni and Così fan tutte.
The Teatro Real's production will be the first time Una cosa rara has been performed in Spain since 1789.
The cast includes María José Moreno, María José Siri, Carlos Chausson, Carlos Mena, and Carlos Álvarez.
The production opens on 12 February 2016, and runs until 28 February.

The Château de Versailles is a royal château in Versailles in the Île-de-France region of France. It is also known as the Palace of Versailles. When the château was built, Versailles was a country village; today, however, it is a suburb of Paris, some twenty kilometers southwest of the French capital. The court of Versailles was the center of political power in France from 1682, when Louis XIV moved from Paris, until the royal family was forced to return to the capital in October 1789 after the beginning of the French Revolution. Versailles is therefore famous not only as a building, but as a symbol of the system of absolute monarchy of the Ancien Régime.

The first phase of the expansion (c. 1661–1678) was designed and supervised by the architect Louis Le Vau. It culminated in the addition of three new wings of stone (the enveloppe), which surrounded Louis XIII's original building on the north, south, and west (the garden side). After Le Vau's death in 1670, the work was taken over and completed by his assistant François d'Orbay. Charles Le Brun designed and supervised the elaborate interior decoration, and André Le Nôtre landscaped the extensive Gardens of Versailles. Le Brun and Le Nôtre collaborated on the numerous fountains, and Le Brun supervised the design and installation of countless statues.

Mansart also built the north and south wings, which encompassed the Grand Apartment on the north and the Hall of Mirrors to the south. Parliament Square is a square at the northwest end of the Palace of Westminster in London. It features a large open green area in the centre with trees to its west and it contains twelve statues of statesmen and other notable individuals. As well as being one of London's main tourist attractions, it is also the place where many demonstrations and protests have been held. The square is overlooked by various official buildings: legislature to the east (in the Houses of Parliament), executive offices to the north (on Whitehall), the judiciary to the west (the Supreme Court), and the church to the south (with Westminster Abbey).
The square was created in 1868 as part of street-widening scheme. The architect responsible was Sir Charles Barry. The buildings surrounding the square are of various styles and varied ages. The oldest is the Grade I listed Westminster Abbey, which was completed in 1745. The 19th-century rebuilding of the Houses of Parliament included the construction of the Clock Tower at the north-eastern corner of the site, which contains the famous bell Big Ben. The Clock Tower is often erroneously referred to by the name of its bell.
The square is planted with grass and dotted with trees and it contains twelve statues of statesmen, each mounted on a pedestal. The Medal of Honor is the highest military decoration that may be awarded by the United States government. It is presented for personal acts of valor above and beyond the call of duty. The medal is awarded by the President of the United States in the name of the U.S. Congress to U.S. military personnel only. There are three versions of the medal, one for the Army, one for the Navy, and one for the Air Force. Personnel of the Marine Corps and Coast Guard receive the Navy version.
U.S. awards including the Medal of Honor do not have titles and while there is no official abbreviation, the most common abbreviations are "MOH" and "MH". The Medal of Honor is often referred to as the Congressional Medal of Honor, but the official name is "Medal of Honor".
The Medal of Honor is bestowed on a member of the United States armed forces who distinguishes himself "conspicuously by gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty while engaged in an action against an enemy of the United States". Due to the nature of its criteria, the medal is often awarded posthumously (more than half have been since 1941).
Members of all branches of the U.S. military are eligible to receive the medal, and each service has a unique design with the exception of the Marine Corps and the Coast Guard, which both use the Navy's medal. The Medal of Honor is the oldest continuously issued combat decoration of the United States armed forces. The Army version has been in use since 1862, with the Navy version coming into use in 1861 and the Air Force and Coast Guard following in 1960. The Medal of Honor was created as a Navy version in 1861 named the "Medal of Valor", and an Army version of the medal named the "Medal of Honor" was established in 1862 to give recognition to men who distinguished themselves "conspicuously by gallantry and intrepidity" in combat with an enemy of the United States.
Because the medal is presented "in the name of Congress", it is often referred to as the "Congressional Medal of Honor".

April is the cruellest month, breeding Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing Memory and desire, stirring Dull roots with spring rain. The Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC) was a Bronze Age civilisation in the northwestern regions of South Asia, lasting from 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE, and in its mature form from 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE. Together with ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia it was one of three early civilisations of the Old World, and of the three the most widespread. It flourished in the basins of the Indus River, which flows through the length of Pakistan, and along a system of perennial, mostly monsoon-fed, rivers that once coursed in the vicinity of the seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra river in northwest India and eastern Pakistan.
An Indus Valley site has been found on the Oxus River at Shortugai in northern Afghanistan, in the Gomal River valley in northwest Pakistan, at Manda, Jammu on the Beas River near Jammu, India, and at Alamgirpur on the Hindon River, only 28 km (17 mi) from Delhi. The southernmost site of the Indus valley civilisation is Daimabad in Maharashtra. Indus Valley sites have been found most often on rivers, but also on the ancient seacoast, for example, Balakot, and on islands, for example, Dholavira. There is evidence of dry river beds overlapping with the Hakra channel in Pakistan and the seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra river in India. Many Indus Valley (or Harappan) sites have been discovered along the Ghaggar-Hakra beds. Among them are: Rupar, Rakhigarhi, Sothi, Kalibangan, Harappa, and Mohenjo-Daro.
According to J. G. Shaffer and D. A. Lichtenstein, the Indus Valley Civilisation "is a good candidate for being the least known of the three great civilizations of the Near East and Egypt". Despite the discovery of the civilisation in the 1920s, it is still relatively unknown in the wider world. The Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) is a commuter rail system in the southeastern part of the U.S. state of New York, stretching from Manhattan to the eastern tip of Suffolk County on Long Island. With an average weekday ridership of 337,800 passengers in 2014, it is the busiest commuter railroad in North America. It is also one of the world's few commuter systems that runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, year-round. It is publicly owned by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which refers to it as MTA Long Island Rail Road, as it does not have a legal name of its own.
The LIRR logo combines the circular MTA logo with the text Long Island Rail Road, and appears on the sides of trains. The LIRR is one of two commuter rail systems owned by the MTA, the other being the Metro-North Railroad in the Hudson Valley, New York and Connecticut. Established in 1834 and having operated continuously since then, it is the oldest US railroad still operating under its original name and charter.

A train station, railway station, railroad station, or depot (see below) is a railway facility where trains regularly stop to load or unload passengers or freight.
It generally consists of at least one track-side platform and a station building (depot) providing such ancillary services as ticket sales and waiting rooms. If a station is on a single-track line, it often has a passing loop to facilitate traffic movements. The smallest stations are most often referred to as "stops" or, in some parts of the world, as "halts" (flag stops).
Stations may be at ground level, underground, or elevated. Connections may be available to intersecting rail lines or other transport modes such as buses, trams or other rapid transit systems.
In the United States, the most common term in contemporary usage is train station. Railway station and railroad station are less frequent; also, American usage makes a distinction between the terms railroad and railway.

Romanian-born German writer Herta Müller has won the 2009 Nobel Prize for Literature.
The Swedish Academy said the 56-year-old author, who emigrated to Germany in 1987, won the award for works that "with the concentration of poetry and the frankness of prose, depicts the landscape of the dispossessed".
Ms Müller, who was born in the Romanian town of Nitzkydorf and speaks German, Romanian and Hungarian, is the 12th woman to win the prize since it was first awarded in 1901.
She is the first German writer to win the prize since Guenter Grass in 1999.
Ms Müller's best-known works include The Passport, The Land of Green Plums and The Appointment.
She has also written several volumes of poetry and essays.
Ms Müller was persecuted for her critical depictions of life in Nicolae Ceausescu's Romania and was banned from publishing in her homeland.
She was allowed to leave for Germany in 1987 with her husband, who is also a writer.
The couple live in Berlin.
The Nobel Prize for Literature is worth 10 million Swedish kronor (£880,000).
The award will be presented at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of prize founder Alfred Nobel's death in 1896.
Last year's winner was French writer Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clezio.

The Texaco New York World's Fair
The Texaco New York World's Fair was a 1964-1965 World's Fair held in Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in the borough of Queens in New York City. It was the largest event held in the park since the 1939-1940 New York World's Fair. Hailing itself as a "universal and international" exposition, the fair's theme was "Peace Through Understanding", dedicated to "Man's Achievement on a Shrinking Globe in an Expanding Universe". American companies dominated the exposition as exhibitors. The theme was symbolized by a 12-story high, stainless-steel model of the earth called the Unisphere, built in the image of a 12-inch wide aluminum model. The fair ran for two six-month seasons, April 22 – October 18, 1964, and April 21 – October 17, 1965. Admission price for adults (13 and older) was $2 in 1964 (equivalent to $15.40 in 2016) but the admission was increased to $2.50 (equivalent to $19.20 in 2016) for the 1965 season.
The fair is best remembered as a showcase of mid-20th-century American culture and technology. The nascent Space Age, with its vista of promise, was well represented. More than 51 million people attended the fair, though fewer than the hoped-for 70 million. It remains a touchstone for many American Baby Boomers, who visited the optimistic fair as children before the turbulent years of the Vietnam War and the Civil Rights Movement.

The Mojave Desert is a desert in the southwestern United States, primarily within southeastern California and southern Nevada, occupying 47,877 sq mi (124,000 km2). It is bordered by the Great Basin Desert to its north and the Sonoran Desert to its south and east. Topographical boundaries include the Tehachapi Mountains to the northwest, the San Gabriel Mountains and San Bernardino Mountains to the south, and the East California Shear Zone to the west. The mountain boundaries are quite distinct since they are outlined by the two largest faults in California – the San Andreas and Garlock faults. The Mojave Desert displays typical basin and range topography. Higher elevations above 2,000 ft (610 m) in the Mojave are commonly referred to as the High Desert; however, Death Valley is the lowest elevation in North America at 282 ft (86 m) below sea level and is one of the hottest places on Earth. The Mojave Desert occupies less than 50,000 sq mi (130,000 km2), making it the smallest of the North American deserts. The Mojave Desert is often referred to as the "high desert", in contrast to the "low desert", the Sonoran Desert to the south. However, the Mojave Desert is generally lower than the Great Basin Desert to the north. The spelling Mojave originates from the Spanish language while the spelling Mohave comes from modern English. Both are used today, although the Mohave Tribal Nation officially uses the spelling Mojave; the word is a shortened form of Hamakhaave, their endonym in their native language, which means 'beside the water'.

The National University of Córdoba is the oldest university of the country and the seventh to be inaugurated in Spanish America. It was founded in 1613 by the Jesuit Order. Heat waves from the northern part of the country bring temperatures above 35 °C (95 °F), yet the city receives enough rain during summer to avoid the semiarid climate classification. Winters are generally mild, though frosts are common and snowfall is not unheard of. Spring and fall are transition seasons characterized by changeable weather.

regression
=============================

This is a simple implementation of functional linear regression.

The code is based on the following paper:

- [Functional linear regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05121)


## Installation

```
pip install git+https://github.com/julien-y-m/functional-linear-regression.git
```


## Usage

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from flr import FunctionalLinearRegression

# Generate data
X = np.random.randn(100, 100)
y = np.random.randn(100)

# Fit the model
model = FunctionalLinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

# Predict
X_test = np.random.randn(10, 100)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

# Plot
plt.scatter(X, y, color='red')
plt.plot(X_test, y_pred, color='blue')
plt.show()
```

Since then, the Great Wall has on and off been rebuilt, maintained, and enhanced; the majority of the existing wall is from the Ming Dynasty.
The Great Wall stretches from Dandong in the east, to Lop Lake in the west, along an arc that roughly delineates the southern edge of Inner Mongolia. Known for his sensuous forms, Rodrigues utilized the alluring qualities of Brazilian wood in his sexy Mole chair and sinuous Sinuoso chaise.
Rodrigues’s work has been featured in exhibitions around the world, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

HEL for 2x660 MW thermal power plant in Telangana
Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) has won an order for setting up a 2x660 MW thermal power plant in Telangana.
Valued at over Rs. 3,500 Crore, the order for setting up the Singareni Thermal Power Project (2x660 MW) expansion at Pegadapalli, has been placed on BHEL by Singareni Collieries Company Limited (SCCL).
BHEL’s scope of work in the project envisages design, engineering, manufacture, supply, erection and commissioning of Steam Turbines, Generators, Boilers, associated Auxiliaries and Electricals, besides state-of-the-art Controls & Instrumentation (C&I) and Electrostatic Precipitators (ESPs).
The equipment for the project will be supplied by various manufacturing units of BHEL located at Trichy, Hyderabad, Ranipet, Haridwar, Bhopal, Bengaluru and Jhansi, while the construction of the plant will be undertaken by the company’s Power Sector – Southern Region.
BHEL has a long-standing partnership with SCCL and has earlier executed 1,210 MW of power plants for the company.
BHEL is India’s largest manufacturer of power generation equipment with an installed base of over 1,85,000 MW of power plant equipment globally.
BHEL is also an active player in the field of environment control equipment and has contracted 93 FGD systems for various thermal power plants till date, out of which 10 have already been commissioned.
BHEL is also the largest supplier of Electrostatic Precipitators in the country with a cumulative contracted quantity of 1004 units, out of which 820 units have been commissioned till date.
BHEL is also the leading supplier of Flue Gas Desulphurization (FGD) systems in the country with a cumulative contracted quantity of 93 units, out of which 10 have been commissioned till date.

William H. Whitfield, 81, of 1000 S. Main St., died at 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, July 10, 2001, at his home.
He was born Jan. 2, 1920, in Crawford County, the son of William and Lillie (Brown) Whitfield. He married Mary E. (Brown) Whitfield on Dec. 24, 1941, in Robinson. She survives.
Mr. Whitfield was a retired employee of the former Marathon Oil Co. He was a member of the First Baptist Church in Robinson. He was a U.S. Army veteran of World War II.
Surviving are his wife, Mary E. Whitfield of Robinson; one son, William H. Whitfield Jr. of Robinson; one daughter, Mary Ann Whitfield of Robinson; one brother, James Whitfield of Robinson; and one sister, Mary Lou Whitfield of Robinson.
He was preceded in death by his parents; one brother, Robert Whitfield; and one sister, Lillie Mae Whitfield.
Funeral services will be at 10 a.m. Friday at the Pulliam Funeral Home in Robinson with the Rev. David Shafer officiating. Burial will be in the Robinson New Cemetery. Visitation will be from 5 to 8 p.m. Thursday at the funeral home.
Memorials may be made to the First Baptist Church in Robinson.
